expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round in this workspace: establishes the per-workload latency of the lean direct-launch architecture versus the PyTorch reference

conclusion.debug_lesson: The seed's own device kernel is only ~3.2us; its 0.10x score came from ~150us of host wrapper cost per call, so on this stack host dispatch, not arithmetic, is the optimization target.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Replaced the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper with a self-contained kernel[grid] implementation and added an explicit strided in-place path, which is also what makes the strided correctness cases pass.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-call Triton JIT dispatch with a pre-bound launcher for the same compiled kernel, re-reading pointer, numel and current stream on every call
plan.code_changes: Dense path: first call per (dtype, data_ptr&15) does a normal kernel[grid] launch and warmup; later calls invoke the already-compiled kernel's generated NPU launcher directly with the per-call data_ptr, numel and current stream (bound via torch_npu._C._npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait, same value as the Triton driver wrapper). Kernel body, BLOCK=8192, strided path and empty/semantic handling unchanged. Added do_not_specialize on n_elements so the reused artifact is valid for any numel.
plan.hypothesis: Nearly all of the remaining per-call latency is Triton JIT dispatch, not device work: the device event is ~3.2us while every workload measured 65-77us, and a tight-loop probe of the pre-bound launcher plus raw-stream read measured 10.0us end to end versus 11.4us for torch.rad2deg_

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing per-call JIT argument binding, specialization, cache-key and global-version bookkeeping (measured ~53us/call versus ~8us for the pre-bound launcher plus ~0.4us for the raw current-stream read) should collapse the fixed per-call cost that made latency nearly size-independent at 65-77us

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed by measurement that the per-call cost was Triton JIT dispatch rather than device work: the pre-bound launcher plus raw current-stream read reproduces the reference's tight-loop cost (10.0us versus 11.4us) and the harness now reports 14.3-14.8us for the nine launch-bound workloads. The three 4096x4096 workloads stay at 76.7-77.1us because BLOCK=8192 leaves them device-bound (measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements at that tile, 0.85TB/s, versus an 18.9us reference at 3.5TB/s).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: removing per-call JIT dispatch collapses the fixed cost that made latency size-independent. Observed: the nine workloads of 1024/65536/1048576 elements dropped from 65.4-65.9us to 14.26-14.78us (speedup 1.21-1.30x against a 17.6-18.7us reference), matching the ~10us tight-loop floor of the pre-bound launcher plus harness measurement overhead. The three 4096x4096 workloads were predicted to be unchanged and were: 76.7/76.8/77.1us (speedup 0.239/0.256/0.374) because there the device, not the launch path, dominates. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.3126 -> 0.8607 (2.75x) and all 36 workloads still pass, so the expectation was met and the residual gap is fully localized to the large-tile device path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Right-size the tile per size class, since the remaining gap is entirely the three 4096x4096 workloads: they are device-bound at 76.7-77.1us with BLOCK=8192 (0.85TB/s measured on target), while the same kernel at BLOCK=32768 measured 29.0us for fp16 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32. Use BLOCK=32768 for the large class, keep 8192 for the mid class and a small tile for the <=2048 class.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this stack the Triton JIT dispatch (binder + specialization + cache key + global-version check, ~53us) is an order of magnitude larger than the kernel (3.2us), so a pre-bound launcher is the primary lever, not the arithmetic. The pre-bound C launcher with an integer pointer costs 7.7us versus 12.9us with a tensor argument, and the raw current-stream read costs 0.44us versus 4.6us through the Triton driver wrapper.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 removed the framework wrapper and fixed strided in-place semantics (0.31x). Round 2 kept the same kernel and tile and only changed how it is launched, which raised the geo_mean to 0.861 and left tile sizing as the single remaining device-side lever.

plan.strategy: Right-size the elementwise tile per size class while keeping the same kernel and pre-bound launch path
plan.code_changes: Added a tile-size ladder selected from numel inside run(): BLOCK=2048 for n<=2048, BLOCK=8192 for n<=131072 (unchanged for the mid class), BLOCK=32768 above that. The block is part of the launch-cache key and is passed to _bind so each class binds its own compiled kernel; kernel body, launch path, strided path and semantics unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound by an undersized tile, not by the launch path: with BLOCK=8192 the on-target probe measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements (0.85TB/s) versus 29.0us at BLOCK=32768 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32 versus a 30.6us reference, while every workload at or below 1048576 elements is launch-bound and unchanged by tile size

expected_effect.mechanism: Amortising each program's prologue/epilogue over a 64KB tile instead of 16KB raises the large-class MTE throughput from the measured 0.85TB/s to 2.3TB/s, cutting the device-bound 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us; the smaller tile for tiny inputs removes wasted masked lanes

conclusion.root_cause: With the launch path fixed, the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by the kernel's per-element vector work at BLOCK=8192. Raising the tile to 32768 lifted the effective throughput from 0.85TB/s to ~2.4TB/s, which is why those workloads dropped to 27.9-31.0us.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: the large class was device-bound by an undersized tile and should drop from 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us, with the launch-bound workloads unchanged. Observed: the three 4096x4096 workloads fell to 27.85us (fp16), 29.91us (bf16) and 31.00us (fp32), i.e. speedups 0.650/0.638/0.929, slightly better than predicted. The nine launch-bound workloads also improved (14.26-14.78us -> 12.91-13.88us, speedup 1.25-1.34x) because the tiny class stopped spreading 1024 elements over 8192 masked lanes and the 1M class moved to a larger tile. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.8607 -> 1.1289 with all 36 workloads passing; the fp32 16M case at 0.93x while fp16/bf16 sit at 0.65x localizes the residual gap to the fp32 intermediate conversion, not to bandwidth.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Switch the low-precision elementwise math to the input dtype: the fp32 upcast/downcast makes the large fp16/bf16 workloads vector-op bound rather than bandwidth bound, which is why fp32 (no conversion) reaches 0.93x while fp16/bf16 reach only 0.65x. Triton's scalar rule already keeps `x * const` in the tensor's dtype, so removing the explicit fp32 round-trip should cut two of the four vector ops.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The harness measures per-iteration throughput with host and device overlapped: the large workloads now report ~28-31us, i.e. the device time alone, not device+host. Tile size is therefore the only lever for the large class and the launch path is the only lever for the rest.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 fixed the host path (0.861x, nine workloads above 1.2x). Round 3 fixed the tile for the device-bound class (1.129x). The remaining asymmetry is that fp32, which has no conversion, is already near reference bandwidth while fp16/bf16 are not.

plan.strategy: Evaluate the elementwise scaling in the input dtype instead of round-tripping fp16/bf16 through fp32
plan.code_changes: Both kernels changed from (x.to(tl.float32) * 57.29577951308232).to(x.dtype) to x * 57.29577951308232. Triton's scalar rule (scalar kind <= tensor kind does not participate in promotion) evaluates this in the input dtype, so fp16/bf16 avoid the fp32 round-trip while fp32 math is bit-identical to before. Launch path, tile ladder, cache keys and control flow unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three large fp32/bf16 cases are limited by the fp32 intermediate conversion rather than by memory traffic: fp32, which needs no conversion, already reaches 0.93x of the reference while otherwise identical fp16 and bf16 kernels reach only 0.650x and 0.638x

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the per-element vector work for the low-precision large tensors (remove upcast and downcast) should move the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 workloads from vector-op bound toward the 4.3TB/s bandwidth already reached by the conversion-free fp32 case

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker — all 5 requests (timing-7, timing-11, timing-3, timing-0 at metrics level; timing-0 again at instruction level) returned status=failed with artifacts=[], metrics={} and summary.stage_count=1. No counters, pipeline utilization or instruction listing were produced for round 4, so no artifact exists to cite; the eval-side observations below are carried in prose instead of evidence entries and remain unverified on

conclusion.root_cause: fp16 has native vector multiply on this backend, so removing the upcast/downcast cut two of four vector ops and raised throughput from 2.4TB/s to 3.2TB/s; bf16 multiply is evidently emulated through fp32 with truncation, so the same edit left its cost unchanged while degrading its accuracy.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: removing the fp32 round-trip moves the low-precision large workloads from vector-op bound toward reference bandwidth, lifting geo_mean. Observed per workload: the fp16 4096x4096 case went 27.85us -> 21.18us (speedup 0.650 -> 0.808) and its contract error became exactly 0, matching the prediction; the fp32 case was unchanged as expected (30.98us, 0.935); but the bf16 4096x4096 case did not move (29.91 -> 29.94us, 0.638) and its error grew from 0.0 to 0.0076 relative. Two of three groups behaved as predicted, so the aggregate only rose 1.1289 -> 1.1342, and the mechanism was only half confirmed.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Apply the input-dtype multiply only to fp16 and restore the fp32 round-trip for bf16 (and keep fp32 as is), selected by a compile-time dtype branch inside the kernel; this keeps the fp16 gain (21.18us, bit-exact) while returning bf16 to exact agreement at the same speed.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Dropping an explicit fp32 round-trip is only free where the backend has native low-precision vector ops: fp16 became bit-identical to the reference and 24% faster on the large case, while bf16 lost accuracy (max relative error 0.0079 in an independent probe, i.e. only 1.26x margin against the 1e-2 gate tolerance) without gaining any speed, which points to bf16 multiply being emulated through fp32 with truncation.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 fixed the launch path, round 3 fixed the tile, round 4 tried dtype-native arithmetic. The fp16 half of that idea is confirmed and should be kept; the bf16 half must be reverted because it trades accuracy for nothing.

plan.strategy: Measure the provided best-so-far seed unchanged to establish the authoritative baseline for this workspace.
plan.code_changes: None. tmp/main.py is byte-identical to the supplied starting point (sha256 3b2c0328b1857ef802e575805c4e25d002ac0166c22fa5cc6804cb1c8d0eeecc).
plan.hypothesis: The seed's pre-bound raw-launcher path plus one-tile-per-program kernels should reproduce the recorded starting score of ~0.767 geomean, with the 4096x4096 cases (fp16/bf16) as the worst workloads and all small cases limited by per-call fixed cost near 17us versus the reference's ~13.4us.

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; establishes the reference point for per-workload latencies against the frozen CANN oracle.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline measured. Two distinct bottlenecks. (1) Fixed per-call cost: the 9 small/medium workloads (1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements, all dtypes) land at 13.49-14.55us versus a reference floor of 11.59-12.02us; the reference is flat across those sizes so both sides are host-issue-bound there, and the candidate's Python fast path (numel/is_contiguous/dtype/data_ptr attribute reads, dict lookup, raw-stream getter, 12-argument raw launcher call) costs ~1.8-2.5us more than the oracle's C++ aclnn entry. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound and dtype-dependent: subtracting each side's own fixed cost gives candidate kernel time ~14.3us (fp16) and ~16.4us (bf16) versus reference ~5.3us and ~7.5us, while fp32 is at parity (~17.5us vs ~17.1us). The paired CANN profile of this exact source explains it: the candidate runs 512 programs of one 32768-element tile each, so every program does a single non-overlapped load-wait-compute-store-wait sequence (aiv_mte2_ratio 0.339, 2029 MTE2 instructions of ~16KB each), whereas the oracle streams ~0.8MB per program over 40 programs with a software-pipelined loop (aiv_mte2_ratio 0.935, 1480 MTE2 instructions of ~22KB each). Per-DMA fixed latency therefore dominates the 512-block launch, and the smaller fp16/bf16 tiles lose more than the 128KB fp32 tiles.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement; baseline geomean 0.80897 with min_speedup 0.61189 at rad2deg_-timing-3. Spread of the 12 timing speedups is bimodal: 0.800-0.930 for the nine small/medium cases and 0.612/0.639 for the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 cases. Raising the two worst cases to reference parity alone multiplies the geomean by ~1.09; removing the whole 1.8-2.5us fixed-cost gap on the six smallest cases multiplies it by ~1.05.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the one-tile-per-program contiguous kernel for large inputs with a program-count-capped streaming kernel (grid ~ num_vectorcore, inner loop over tiles, multi-buffered so load/compute/store overlap) to amortise the per-DMA fixed latency over ~10-50 tiles per program, which is the mechanism the 0.935 mte2-ratio oracle uses; keep the small-input path unchanged so attribution stays clean.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A bounded target probe showed the seed's host path at ~13.9us and the reference at ~13.5us with per-call-sync costing ~50us, confirming the harness measures an async throughput loop rather than a synchronised per-call figure; the probe environment was per-program-overhead-bound rather than bandwidth-bound (identical 56us for fp16 and fp32 at 16M elements), so absolute probe numbers cannot be compared across environments and only in-process relative comparisons are usable.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline only. Next step splits the two bottlenecks: device architecture first (three worst workloads, largest deterministic headroom), then host-side per-call trimming.

plan.strategy: Replace the one-tile-per-program launch for large inputs with a single-wave persistent streaming launch capped by the device's vector-core count.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel: pid strides over tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop, so one program covers a strip of tiles. Added _num_vec_core (queried from driver.active.utils.get_device_properties -> num_vectorcore = 40) and _stream_grid(), which launches min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore) programs. Inputs above 131072 elements now use this kernel with BLOCK=16384; the <=131072 paths and the strided path are byte-identical to round 1. Launcher cache is keyed by (path, dtype, data_ptr & 15) with the tile size stored in the entry.
plan.hypothesis: At 4096x4096 the candidate's device time is dominated by the number of programs rather than by bytes: 16.7M/32768 gives 512 programs = 12.8 sequential waves, and the candidate's fp16 and fp32 times are nearly dtype-independent (27.8us vs 31.0us for twice the bytes) while the oracle's scale with bytes. Collapsing the launch to one wave of streaming programs should cut the fp16/bf16 cases most and leave the nine host-bound small/medium cases untouched.

expected_effect.mechanism: Replacing 512 one-tile programs (12.8 sequential waves over 40 vector cores, each wave paying a full program prologue plus a load-wait-compute-store-drain cycle) with a single wave of <=40 streaming programs that multi-buffer consecutive tiles inside one program removes the per-program dispatch/drain cost that the paired profile attributes to the aiv_mte2_ratio of 0.339 versus the oracle's 0.935.

conclusion.root_cause: The hypothesis that the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by per-program dispatch cost is refuted. The streaming kernel launched 40 programs (one wave) of 16384-element tiles instead of 512 programs of 32768-element tiles, and the fp16/bf16 cases became slower, while the fp32 case also degraded. Halving the tile size halved the bytes moved per transport step, so the loop gained nothing from having one program per core and lost transport efficiency; the dominant cost is bytes per transport step, not the number of programs.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: geomean increase driven by the three 4096x4096 workloads. Observed: geomean 0.78141 versus 0.80897 at round 1 (is_new_best false). The two cleanly comparable workloads, whose reference latency was unchanged in this run (rad2deg_-timing-3 reference 17.033->17.060us, rad2deg_-timing-7 19.132->19.193us), moved the wrong way: timing-3 27.837->30.205us (speedup 0.612->0.565) and timing-7 29.923->32.345us (0.639->0.593), i.e. about 8% slower. The rest of the run was degraded by environment noise rather than by the change: rad2deg_-timing-8/9/10 run byte-identical code to round 1 (n=1024/65536/1048576 use the untouched contiguous path) yet moved 13.79/13.49/13.84->16.13/16.32/15.30us, and the rad2deg_-timing-11 reference itself rose 28.79->39.67us. Interpretation: per-program dispatch/drain overhead was not the limiter; transport efficiency follows bytes per transport step, and replacing a 32768-element tile by a 16384-element tile inside a loop cut the per-step transport size in half, which cost more than the saved program count. The round-1 kernel already keeps every tile at 64KB (fp16) / 128KB (fp32), the largest that fits the 192KB UB budget.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Abandon program-count reduction for the large path and revert to the round-1 one-tile-per-program kernel (BLOCK=32768). Spend the next round on the nine host-issue-bound small/medium workloads instead: quantify the pure raw-launcher cost versus the Python bookkeeping around it with a bounded probe, then cut the per-call Python work (single cached entry per (dtype, alignment), no size-class branching, precomputed grid expression) so the fixed cost moves from 13.5-14.5us toward the 11.6-12.0us oracle floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Bounded probes on this target show the debug-job device is memory-contended relative to the evaluator (identical 16.7M kernels take 55-65us there versus 27.8-31.0us under eval), so only in-process relative comparisons across the same run are usable; absolute probe numbers must never be compared with eval numbers.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 assumed the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 gap came from program-count/wave overhead. That is now measured false. The next hypothesis moves to the other bottleneck measured in round 1: the fixed per-call host cost of the nine small/medium workloads, where the candidate is at 13.5-14.5us against an 11.6-12.0us oracle floor and the device kernel is fully hidden.

plan.strategy: Cut the per-call Python bookkeeping around the pre-bound raw launcher for the nine host-issue-bound small and medium workloads.
plan.code_changes: Host wrapper only; both kernels unchanged. Replaced the single cache keyed by (dtype, align, block) with two dicts keyed by (dtype, data_ptr & 15) that carry the tile size, so the hot path builds a 2-tuple key and picks the dict with one comparison instead of a three-way tile-size chain. Removed _BLOCK_TINY (2048): inputs <=131072 now use tile 8192, above that tile 32768 as before. The stream getter _npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait is now called directly on the module-level device instead of through the _stream_fn lambda, saving one Python frame per call; the device is (re)resolved in the cold bind path.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of the twelve timing workloads (1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements for fp16/bf16/fp32) are limited by fixed per-call host cost, not by device work: the reference is flat at 11.6-12.0us across all three sizes while the candidate sits at 13.5-14.5us. A bounded probe split the candidate call into 8.93us for the raw launcher alone and 3.28us of Python wrapper, so trimming the wrapper moves those nine workloads toward the oracle floor. plan.strategy: Expose the large 2-byte in-place loop as a two-pointer operation so the compiler can keep consecutive tiles in flight.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK) which strides tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop and stores through y_ptr. For inputs above 131072 elements whose element size is 2 bytes, the cold path binds this kernel with BLOCK=16384 and a grid of min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore), passing the same buffer as both pointer arguments; every other case (2-byte and 4-byte inputs <=131072, all 4-byte large inputs) keeps the round-3 contiguous kernel unchanged. The small-input hot path was left byte-identical, and the 4-byte large path still uses one tile of 32768 per program.
plan.hypothesis: rad2deg_-timing-3 and rad2deg_-timing-7 are stuck near 0.61-0.64 while rad2deg_-timing-11 (fp32) reaches 0.93, and round 2 showed their per-byte transport cost is unchanged by program count or tile size, so they are limited by transport/arithmetic overlap rather than by tiling. Triton cannot overlap an in-place loop because the store and the following load share one base pointer. Giving the compiler two pointer arguments over the same storage should restore that overlap for 2-byte data without touching the fp32 case or any host-bound case.

expected_effect.mechanism: With one pointer serving as both load and store source the next iteration's load must be assumed to alias the previous iteration's store, so tiles are serialised and the transport engine idles; two distinct pointer arguments let consecutive tiles be in flight together, which is the overlap the oracle's 0.935 MTE2-active profile exhibits against this kernel's 0.339.

conclusion.root_cause: Passing the in-place buffer as two distinct pointer arguments let the compiler stop serialising consecutive tiles, which removed the transport idle time on the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads and confirmed that their deficit was lack of load/store overlap, not tiling, program count, masking, or arithmetic precision. The round's aggregate regression is entirely a shared host-side environment shift of ~3.5us that hit workloads whose code is byte-identical to round 3, so the ledger's cross-run geomean comparison rejects an otherwise correct device optimisation.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: a geomean increase from restoring transport/arithmetic overlap on the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads. The mechanism was confirmed strongly: rad2deg_-timing-3 0.610->0.962 (27.846->17.625us against an unchanged 16.950us oracle, a 37% cut) and rad2deg_-timing-7 0.637->1.069 (29.913->17.837us against 19.059us, now faster than the oracle). The untouched fp32 control rad2deg_-timing-11 stayed at 0.928 (30.974us) and all three oracle latencies for the large cases were unchanged (16.95/19.06/28.73us versus round 3's 16.99/19.07/28.82us), so the device result is clean. The aggregate still fell, 0.89785->0.83819, because all nine small/medium workloads shifted by a uniform +3.4 to +3.9us. That shift is not attributable to the change: rad2deg_-timing-10 is fp32 at 1048576 elements, cannot enter the new 2-byte path, and moved 13.478->17.180us, the same as rad2deg_-timing-0 (1024 elements, untouched small path, 13.270->16.153us) and rad2deg_-timing-4 (13.326->17.183us). The oracle for those workloads moved only +2.5% (12.83-13.62us -> 13.28-13.76us), and the resulting ~17.1us level matches the campaign's first measurement of the untouched seed. A request_retest of this round reproduced every figure with empty drift, so the shift is stable for this run rather than transient, but it is shared with the environment and not caused by the kernel. Excluding that shift, round 4's small/medium per-workload ratios are unchanged from round 3, so the round is a net device improvement that the aggregate geomean cannot see.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Ship the union of rounds 3 and 4: keep round 3's host path exactly (it holds the nine small/medium workloads at 0.918-1.002) and add round 4's two-pointer streaming kernel for the >131072-element 2-byte path only, leaving the fp32 large path and all small paths untouched. The two rounds' per-workload ratios are measured in mutually consistent environments (each run's oracle latencies agree to 0.4%), so their product gives an expected geomean near 0.97: 0.971, 1.000, 0.980, 0.962, 0.994, 0.918, 0.956, 1.069, 1.002, 0.960, 0.952, 0.928.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A uniform additive shift across workloads that run byte-identical code is the signature of a host-side environment change, not of a candidate change. Round 4 is the demonstration: the two-pointer kernel only touches the >131072-element 2-byte path, yet every small/medium workload moved by the same ~3.5us, including rad2deg_-timing-10 which is fp32 and cannot enter that path. Comparing per-workload ratios and the oracle's own latencies, rather than the aggregate geomean alone, separated a real 36-68% device win from a shared environment shift.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Three mechanisms for the 2-byte 4096x4096 deficit were tried in order: program-count/wave reduction (round 2, refuted), transport granularity and arithmetic precision (probes, no effect), and finally load/store aliasing as the blocker for pipelining (round 4, confirmed with a 37% cut on fp16 and a win over the oracle on bf16). The host-side lever found in round 3 remains the single largest measured gain of the session at +11% geomean.
